dagger.e: From Middle English daggere, daggare, dagard, probably adapted from Old French dague (1229), related to Occitan, Italian, Spanish daga, Dutch dagge, German Degen, Middle Low German dagge (“knife's point”), Old Norse daggarðr, Danish daggert, Faroese daggari, Welsh dager, dagr, Breton dac. In English attested from the 1380s.
dagger.g: A stabbing weapon, similar to a sword but with a short, double-edged blade.
A timber placed diagonally in a ship's frame.

daily.e: From Middle English dayly, from Old English dæġlīċ, from Proto-West Germanic *dagalīk, from Proto-Germanic *dagalīkaz (“daily”), equivalent to day + -ly.
daily.g: That occurs or attends every day, or at least every working day.

daily.e: From Middle English dayly, from Old English *dæġlīċe (found only as dæġhwāmlīċe), equivalent to day + -ly.

dainty.e: From Middle English deynte (as noun), from Old French deintié, from Latin dignitātem.

dale.e: From Middle English dale, from Old English dæl, from Proto-West Germanic *dal, from Proto-Germanic *dalą.
dale.g: A valley, often in an otherwise hilly area.

dam.e: From Middle English dam, from Old English *damm, from Proto-West Germanic *damm, from Proto-Germanic *dammaz.
dam.g: A structure placed across a flowing body of water to stop the flow or part of the flow, generally for purposes such as retaining or divertin
Female parent, mother, generally regarding breeding of animals.

damage.e: From Middle English damage, from Old French damage, from Vulgar Latin *damnāticum from Classical Latin damnum. Largely displaced native Middle English scath (whence unscathed).
damage.g: Injury or harm; the condition or measure of something not being intact.

damn.e: From Middle English dampnen, from Old French damner, from Latin damnāre (“to condemn, inflict loss upon”), from damnum (“loss”).

damnable.e: From Middle English dampnable, from Old French dampnable, from Latin damnābilis. By surface analysis, damn + -able.

damnation.e: From Middle English dampnacioun, from Old French dampnacion, from Latin damnatio.
damnation.g: The state of being damned; condemnation; openly expressed disapprobation.

damsel.e: From Middle English dameisele, from Old French damoisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, a diminutive from Classical Latin domina (“mistress, lady”), from dominus, from *demh₂-.

dan.e: From Middle English dan, daun, dam (“lord”), from Anglo-Norman daun, daunz and Old French dan, dam, from Latin dominus.
dan.g: A title of honour or respect similar to "master" or "Sir", used of historical and legendary figures of the past.
A rank of black belt in martial arts.

dance.e: From Middle English dauncen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman dauncer, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre, of uncertain origin.
dance.g: A sequence of rhythmic steps or movements usually performed to music, for pleasure or as a form of social interaction.

dancer.e: From Middle English dauncer, dawncere, dancere, equivalent to dance + -er.
dancer.g: A person who dances, usually as a hobby, an occupation, or a profession.

dancing.e: From dance + -ing. The sense "dance club" is from French dancing, a pseudo-anglicism derived from English dance + -ing.
dancing.g: The activity of taking part in a dance.

danger.e: From Middle English daunger (“power, dominion, peril”), from Anglo-Norman dangier, from Old French dangier, alteration of Old French dongier (due to association with Latin damnum (“damage”)) from Vulgar Latin *dominiārium (“authority, power”) from Latin dominus (“lord, master”).
danger.g: Exposure to likely harm; risk of death or serious injury.

dangerous.e: From Middle English daungerous (“difficult, severe, domineering, arrogant, fraught with danger”), dangerous, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French dangereus (“threatening, difficult”), from dangier. Equivalent to danger + -ous.

dangle.e: Uncertain, but likely of North Germanic origin, akin to Danish dingle, dangle, Swedish dangla (“to swing about”), Norwegian dangla, perhaps via North Frisian dangeln; all possibly related to Old Norse dengja (“to hit”).
dangle.g: To hang loosely with the ability to swing.

dapple.e: Uncertain. The noun and verb are both later attested likely as back-formations.
dapple.g: A mottled marking, usually in clusters.

dare.e: From Middle English durren, from Old English durran, from Proto-West Germanic *durʀan, from Proto-Germanic *durzaną (“to dare”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰedʰórse (“to dare”), reduplicated stative of the root *dʰers- (“to be bold, to dare”), an *-s- extension of *dʰer- (“to hold, support”).
dare.g: To have enough courage (to do something).

dare.e: From Middle English daren, from Old English darian.
dare.g: To stare stupidly or vacantly; to gaze as though amazed or terrified.

daric.e: From Ancient Greek δᾱρεικός (dāreikós), from Old Persian *darikah. Considered by classical authors to be from Δαρεῖος (Dareîos, “Darius”) who standardized the coinage as such, but this is a folk etymology.
daric.g: A gold coin from Persian Empire, introduced by Darius the Great (522-486 BC) and used until Alexander the Great's invasion (330 BC).

dark.e: From Middle English derk, from Old English deorc, from Proto-West Germanic *derk (“dark”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerg- (“dim, dull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“dull, dirty”).
dark.g: Having an absolute or (more often) relative lack of light.

dark.e: From Middle English derk, derke, dirke, dyrke, from the adjective (see above), or possibly from an unrecorded Old English *dierce, *diercu (“dark, darkness”).
dark.g: A complete or (more often) partial absence of light.

darken.e: From Middle English derkenen, dirkenen, from Old English *deorcnian, *diercnian (“to darken”), from Proto-West Germanic *dirkinōn (“to darken”), equivalent to dark + -en.
darken.g: To make dark or darker by reducing light.

darkish.e: From Middle English derkish, derkissh, derkyss; equivalent to dark + -ish.

darkly.e: From Middle English derkly, derkely, derkliche, derkeliche; equivalent to dark + -ly.
darkly.g: With insufficient light for easy discernment or comprehension.

darkly.e: From Middle English derkely, equivalent to dark + -ly.

darkness.e: From Middle English derknesse, from Old English deorcnes; equivalent to dark + -ness.
darkness.g: The state of being dark; lack of light; the absolute or comparative absence of light.

darling.e: By surface analysis, dear + -ling (suffix meaning ‘immature; small’).
darling.g: Often used as an affectionate term of address: a person who is very dear to one.

dart.e: From Middle English dart, from Old French dart, dard (“dart”), from Medieval Latin dardus, from Frankish *darōþu (“dart, spear”), from Proto-Germanic *darōþuz (“dart, spear”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerh₃- (“to leap, spring”).
dart.g: A pointed missile weapon, intended to be thrown by the hand; for example, a short lance or javelin.

dart.e: From Middle English darten, from the noun (see above).
dart.g: To throw with a sudden effort or thrust; to hurl or launch.

darts.g: A game or sport in which darts are thrown at a board, and points are scored depending on where the darts land.

dash.e: From Middle English daschen, dassen, from Danish daske (“to slap, strike”), related to Swedish daska (“to smack, slap, spank”), of obscure origin.
dash.g: Any of the following symbols: ‒ (figure dash), – (en dash), — (em dash), or ― (horizontal bar).

date.e: From Middle English date, from Old French date, datil, datille, from Latin dactylus (likely via Old Provençal datil), from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”) (from the resemblance of the date to a human finger), probably a folk-etymological alteration of a word from a Semitic source such as Arabic دَقَل (daqal, “variety of date palm”).
date.g: The fruit of the date palm, Phoenix dactylifera, somewhat in the shape of an olive, containing a soft, sweet pulp and enclosing a hard kerne

date.e: From Middle English date, from Old French date, from Late Latin data, from Latin datus (“given”), past participle of dare (“to give”); from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”).
date.g: The addition to a writing, inscription, coin, etc., which specifies the time (especially the day, month, and year) when the writing or inscr

daub.e: From Middle English daub (noun), from Middle English dauben (“to plaster or whitewash; cover with clay; bespatter”, verb), from Old Northern French dauber (“to whitewash; plaster”), of uncertain origin. Probably from Latin dealbāre (“to whiten thoroughly”), which would make it a doublet of dealbate.
daub.g: Excrement or clay used as a bonding material in construction.

daughter.e: From Middle English doghter, doughter, from Old English dohtor (“daughter”), from Proto-West Germanic *dohter, from Proto-Germanic *duhtēr, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr.

daughter-in-law.e: From Middle English doghter in lawe; equivalent to daughter + -in-law.

dawn.e: From Middle English dawnen, either a back-formation from dawnynge or a modification of dawen (“to dawn”) after it.
dawn.g: To begin to brighten with daylight.

dawning.e: From Middle English dawnynge, an alteration of dawing, under the influence of North Germanic cognates (compare Swedish, Danish dagning).

day.e: From Middle English day, from Old English dæġ, from Proto-West Germanic *dag, from Proto-Germanic *dagaz (“day”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”).
day.g: The time when the Sun is above the horizon and it lights the sky.

daybreak.g: The beginning of the day; the first moment of daylight.

daylight.e: From Middle English daye-lighte, dey liȝht, dailiȝt, day-liht, dai-liht (also as days lyȝt, daies liht), equivalent to day + light.
daylight.g: The natural light that is ambient in daytime, being mostly sunlight (both direct and indirect, on either sunny days or cloudy days).

days.e: From Middle English dayes, dawes, from Old English dagas, from Proto-Germanic *dagōs, *dagōz, plural of *dagaz, equivalent to day + -s (plural ending).
days.g: A particular time or period of vague extent.

dayspring.e: From Middle English dai spring, equivalent to day + spring.
dayspring.g: The beginning of the day, or first appearance of light; the dawn; daybreak.

dazzling.g: Extremely bright, especially so as to blind the eyes temporarily; bright to the degree that dazzles.
